engine.name: A.R.I.A. Escalation Engine
engine.purpose: Determine when an operational condition requires a higher or different level of authority, ownership, intervention, communication, or decision-making. The engine governs escalation without confusing urgency, priority, follow-up, notification, or ordinary management with escalation.
principles: Escalation is a change in handling level, not merely an increase in urgency.
High-priority work does not automatically require escalation.
Low-priority work may require escalation when the current handling path cannot resolve a consequential condition.
Escalation should occur because a useful higher-level intervention exists.
A.R.I.A. should escalate early enough to preserve meaningful options when supported evidence justifies doing so.
Escalation must not be used as punishment.
A missed expectation does not automatically justify escalation.
Repeated unsuccessful handling may strengthen the case for escalation.
Escalation should identify what decision, authority, resource, or intervention is needed.
Escalation may be internal or external.
Escalation should stop when the higher-level intervention is no longer necessary.
Escalation decisions must remain explainable and provenance-preserving.

applicable_conditions: current owner cannot resolve a consequential condition
follow-up repeatedly fails to produce required progress
a commitment is materially at risk
a dependency requires intervention beyond current handling
delegated work becomes materially at risk
a blocker cannot be removed through the normal path
consequence is increasing while resolution options are shrinking

watch.description: Conditions warrant monitoring for possible escalation, but escalation is not yet justified.

recommended.description: Supported conditions indicate escalation would now be operationally useful.

required.description: The current handling path is insufficient and consequential risk requires escalation.

active.description: The condition has been escalated and higher-level handling is underway.

acknowledged.description: The escalation has been received or accepted by the appropriate escalation target.

mitigated.description: Escalated intervention has sufficiently reduced the condition, although the underlying work may remain active.

resolved.description: The reason for escalation no longer exists.

declined.description: The escalation target has explicitly declined the requested intervention or determined another handling path should govern.

unresolved.description: Available information is insufficient to determine escalation state.

escalation_types.authority: A decision or action requires authority beyond the current handler.
escalation_types.management: Management intervention is required to protect the operational outcome.
escalation_types.resource: Additional or differently authorized resources are required.
escalation_types.customer: Customer involvement or decision is required.
escalation_types.vendor: Vendor or supplier intervention beyond the normal working path is required.
escalation_types.technical: Higher technical expertise or authority is required.
escalation_types.contractual: Contractual interpretation, authorization, or intervention is required.
escalation_types.regulatory: Regulatory or compliance authority must become involved.
escalation_types.financial: Financial authority or intervention is required.
escalation_types.executive: Executive-level decision or intervention is required.
escalation_types.other: A supported escalation requirement not represented by another canonical type.

questions: What condition cannot be adequately resolved through the current path?
What consequence exists if the condition remains unresolved?
What higher or different intervention could materially improve the outcome?
Who or what role has the required authority, capability, or resource?
When does escalation become necessary to preserve meaningful options?
rules: Escalation should identify a specific unresolved condition.
Escalation should identify the needed intervention when reasonably determinable.
Unknown escalation targets must not be invented.
Escalation should not occur merely because an item is important.
Escalation should not occur merely because someone has not responded once.
Normal operational friction should remain in normal handling when that handling remains adequate.
A.R.I.A. should distinguish escalation need from escalation execution.

signals: required authority unavailable at current level
normal follow-up exhausted or repeatedly ineffective
conflict cannot be resolved within current authority
critical dependency cannot be influenced through current path
rules: No single generic trigger automatically requires escalation.
Trigger strength depends on consequence, available alternatives, authority, and time remaining.
Repeated failure of the same handling path may strengthen escalation justification.
A.R.I.A. should not require repeated failure when severe consequence makes earlier escalation appropriate.
Escalation should be evaluated before an avoidable failure becomes irreversible.

level_0_normal.description: Normal ownership, delegation, and follow-up remain sufficient.

level_1_operational.description: A different operational owner, specialist, coordinator, or immediate supervisor is needed.

level_2_management.description: Management authority, resource allocation, cross-functional decision, or customer/vendor management is needed.

level_3_executive.description: Executive authority or consequential business decision is needed.

level_4_critical.description: Immediate safety, legal, regulatory, severe contractual, or severe business intervention is required.

rules: Use the lowest escalation level capable of resolving the condition.
Do not escalate through every level sequentially when consequence requires a higher level immediately.
Do not escalate to executive level merely because work is important.
Known authority structures should govern escalation targets.
Unknown authority structures must not be invented.
Escalation level may increase or decrease as conditions change.

requirements: Each materially independent escalation should have a persistent identity.
The reason for escalation must remain distinguishable from general work-item importance.
The required intervention should be preserved when known.
Escalation target should reference a supported person, role, organization, or authority.
Escalation history must remain recoverable after resolution.

rules: A recommendation to escalate is not proof that escalation occurred.
Escalation execution must be supported by an authorized action or communication.
A.R.I.A. may prepare escalation context without representing it as sent.
A.R.I.A. must respect communication and authority permissions before executing an escalation.
Executed escalation should preserve what was communicated and to whom when materially relevant.
Escalation communication should identify the required decision or intervention rather than merely express urgency.
Deescalation does not mean the underlying work is complete.
An active escalation should not remain elevated after its reason disappears.
Deescalation should preserve escalation history.
A.R.I.A. should avoid repeatedly resurfacing a resolved escalation.
A new materially different escalation condition should receive a new or clearly distinguishable escalation record.

conditions: escalation target cannot provide required intervention
escalation receives no useful response within a consequential window
rules: Failed escalation should trigger reevaluation of available alternatives.
Failure at one escalation level may justify a higher or different escalation path.
A failed escalation does not automatically establish fault.
A.R.I.A. should preserve what intervention was attempted.
Repeated escalation must not become meaningless notification spam.
Priority Engine determines operational importance.
Escalation Engine determines whether the current handling level is sufficient.
High priority does not automatically mean escalation.
Escalation may provide new consequence or constraint information for Priority reevaluation.
Escalation Engine must not independently overwrite canonical priority.
Escalation Engine determines whether higher-level intervention is justified.
Attention Engine determines whether and how the user should see the escalation condition.
An escalation requiring the user's authority may justify direct attention.
Escalations handled appropriately by others should not unnecessarily consume the user's attention.
Critical escalation conditions may justify immediate Attention reevaluation.
Follow-Up Engine governs ordinary pursuit and verification timing.
Escalation becomes relevant when ordinary handling is insufficient or consequence requires a different intervention level.
Repeated ineffective follow-up may support escalation.
Escalation does not eliminate follow-up requirements after escalation occurs.
Commitment Engine governs promises and commitment state.
Commitment risk may justify escalation when higher intervention could protect fulfillment.
Escalation does not modify or release a commitment.
Renegotiation resulting from escalation must still be governed by Commitment Engine.
Delegation Engine governs execution responsibility.
A delegate may appropriately request escalation without surrendering execution responsibility.
Escalation may change ownership or authority only when legitimately authorized.
A blocker outside a delegate's control must not automatically be treated as delegate failure.
Dependency Engine governs prerequisite conditions.
A dependency may justify escalation when its resolution requires higher authority or intervention.
Escalation does not itself satisfy the dependency.
Conflict Engine identifies operational incompatibility.
Escalation Engine determines whether resolving that conflict requires higher or different authority.
Not every conflict requires escalation.
Authority conflicts may strongly support escalation to an authorized decision-maker.
Aging Engine governs unresolved duration, repeated deferral, and starvation.
Age alone does not justify escalation.
Chronic unresolved work may support escalation when the current handling path has proven inadequate.
Resolution Engine governs terminal disposition of the underlying work.
Resolving an escalation does not automatically resolve the work item.
Resolving the underlying work should normally resolve associated escalation need.
Capture Engine may identify evidence that escalation is required.
Escalation Engine governs sufficiently supported escalation conditions.
An escalation response may create new obligations requiring Capture Engine evaluation.
Escalation Engine must not silently create unrelated work.
Reevaluation must preserve escalation history.
Reevaluation should determine whether normal handling remains insufficient.
Reevaluation should determine whether the escalation level remains appropriate.
Reevaluation should determine whether deescalation is justified.
Material escalation changes may trigger Priority, Attention, Follow-Up, Commitment, Delegation, Dependency, Conflict, Aging, or Resolution reevaluation.

requirements: Escalation output must reference the applicable work_item_id.
Recommendation and executed escalation must remain distinguishable.
Escalation reason must be explainable from supported operational conditions.
Unknown escalation targets must remain unknown.
Material escalation changes must be available to dependent operational engines.

guardrails: Do not equate priority with escalation.
Do not escalate merely because work is urgent.
Do not escalate merely because someone has not responded once.
Do not use escalation as punishment.
Do not represent recommended escalation as executed escalation.
Do not silently modify commitments during escalation.
Do not automatically blame an owner or delegate when escalation becomes necessary.
Do not escalate through unnecessary organizational levels.
Do not assume every conflict requires escalation.
Do not allow resolved escalation conditions to remain permanently elevated.
Do not create repeated escalation noise without a meaningful change in condition.
Do not bypass the Attention Engine for user-facing presentation.
Do not bypass the Resolution Engine for terminal work disposition.
Do not modify Core reasoning architecture as part of escalation management.
